displayQuote: Raise your words, not voice. It is rain that grows flowers, not thunder

meta.title: Who really said "Raise your words, not voice. It is rain that grows flowers, not thunder"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Rumi scholars can’t find this line anywhere in his works. It’s a modern inspirational aphorism pinned on Rumi — no Persian source, no documented translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Raise your words, not voice. It is rain that grows flowers, not thunder'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to Rumi, but leading Rumi scholars don’t recognize it and it’s in none of his works. A modern feel-good line, not a documented Rumi verse.

answer.label: Not Rumi — an unsourced modern aphorism
answer.authorDates: Line has no documented author; falsely credited to Rumi, 1207–1273
answer.sourceLine: This gentle-rain aphorism is pinned on Rumi across posters, Pinterest and quote sites, but when journalists asked Rumi scholars Fatemah Keshavarz and Franklin Lewis ↗, neither could confirm it: Keshavarz did not recognize the line, and Lewis found it thematically consistent with Rumi’s tone yet could not say it was his without intensive research. It appears in none of his major works (the Masnavi, the Divan-i Shams, or popular anthologies), and no Persian source or translation has ever been cited; the traceable trail is entirely modern inspirational media.

source.excerpt: Raise your words, not voice. It is rain that grows flowers, not thunder.
trail: The line spreads mainly through inspirational media and quote aggregators; Goodreads lists it under Rumi ↗ with no book source, noting quotes “are added by the community and are not verified.”
When journalists pressed for a source, Rumi scholar Fatemah Keshavarz said “I actually don’t know this line” ↗, and it turned up in none of the standard collections that were checked.
It does not appear on Wikiquote’s sourced Rumi page ↗, which draws on the Masnavi and Divan-i Shams — consistent with it not being a genuine Rumi verse.
The wider pattern is documented by Rozina Ali in The New Yorker ↗: much popular ‘Rumi’ in English is loose interpretation or invention, not translation.
source.excerptNote: Also circulates as “Raise your words, not your voice. It’s rain that grows flowers, not thunder” — the wording drifts between versions, a hallmark of an unsourced quote.

source.rightsNote: Because the line cannot be tied to any Rumi work or any identified author, its origin and first-publication date are unknown, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. Rumi’s own 13th-century Persian is long in the public domain, but that is irrelevant here: this is not a documented Rumi text, and the modern English wording has no known source to classify.

author.name: Rumi
author.heading: About Rumi
author.metaLine: 1207–1273 · Persian poet, Islamic scholar & Sufi mystic
author.bio: Jalal ad-Din Muhammad Rumi was a 13th-century Persian poet, jurist and Sufi mystic whose Masnavi and Divan-i Shams are cornerstones of Persian literature. In the West he is among the best-selling poets — largely through loose interpretive renderings that strip his Islamic context, which is exactly how lines he never wrote circulate under his name. Because his popular English ‘quotes’ are so often paraphrase or invention, an unsourced feel-good line like this one is suspect by default.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. Earliest documented discussion: Ashley Reese, Jezebel, “Did Tiffany Trump Post a Fake Rumi Quote on Instagram? Jezebel Investigates” (7 May 2019), quoting Rumi scholars unable to confirm the line.

copyAttribution: Misattributed to Rumi — no documented source; Rumi scholars do not recognize the line and it appears in none of his works.

misattribution.heading: Why this isn’t really Rumi
misattribution.intro: The quote is one of the most-shared “Rumi” lines online, yet it fails the most basic test: no one can point to where Rumi wrote it. It is a modern inspirational aphorism that acquired his name for prestige.

items.why: Asked by journalists, Rumi specialists Fatemah Keshavarz and Franklin Lewis ↗ could not confirm it: Keshavarz did not recognize the line and noted that “quotes without reference are often suspicious,” while Lewis found it thematically consistent with Rumi’s tone but could not verify it without intensive research. It was found in none of the collections checked (The Love Poems of Rumi, A Year with Rumi, the Masnavi).

items.who: “The Love Poems of Rumi” and similar anthologies
items.why: Some posts name a specific Rumi book, but the line does not appear in those volumes ↗ — a citation offered but not confirmable is a classic fake-quote tell.

misattribution.truthLine: Best read as an anonymous modern aphorism: consistent in tone with Sufi imagery, but with no Persian original, no translator and no scholar able to place it — part of the broader “Rumi” that isn’t Rumi ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line went viral partly through celebrity and political shares — a 2019 Instagram post by Tiffany Trump prompted Jezebel to actually ask Rumi scholars whether it was real. Their answer, in effect: nobody can find it.

It endures because it sounds like Rumi — rain, flowers, gentleness over force. But sounding right is how misattributions survive: the imagery is generically ‘Sufi’ enough that few readers demand a chapter and verse that doesn’t exist.
context.pull: Scholars checked the Masnavi, the Divan and the popular anthologies. The line is in none of them.
